sections.title: Why sine won't invert: the many-to-one trap & related topics

board_events.text: Which angle has a sine of one half?
First instinct: $30^\circ = \tfrac{\pi}{6}$. But $150^\circ$ works too, and $390^\circ$, $510^\circ$, $-330^\circ$...
Sine sends infinitely many angles to the same value. It is many-to-one.
Many-to-one is fatal for inversion: an inverse must return exactly ONE answer.

board_events.caption: One sine value, infinitely many angles

board_events.text: Fix: shrink sine's domain to a stretch where it is one-to-one and still sweeps all of $[-1,1]$.
The agreed stretch: $\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$. Now 'sine equals one half' has ONE honest answer: $\tfrac{\pi}{6}$.
That chosen stretch is the principal value branch, the official platform.
Two facts to lock in right now
Fact one: the branch is a choice, but a fixed, canonical one.
Other one-to-one stretches exist (even $[2\pi, 3\pi]$ for cosine), yet the world agrees on one, so $\sin^{-1}\tfrac{1}{2}$ means the same everywhere.
Fact two: the output is an ANGLE, and it is trapped inside its branch. Always.
So if you ever produce $\sin^{-1}(\text{something}) = \tfrac{2\pi}{3}$, you have already erred: $120^\circ$ lies outside $\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$.

board_events.text: Sine and cosine inverse take inputs in $[-1,1]$; tangent and cotangent inverse accept every real number.
Secant and cosecant inverse need $|x| \ge 1$: a reciprocal can never land strictly between minus one and one.
Tan's cage is open at $\pm\tfrac{\pi}{2}$; cot's is open at $0$ and $\pi$: undefined there.
Sec drops $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ (cosine zero); cosec drops $0$ (sine zero). The deleted point is the tell.
Three patterns, not eighteen facts: the zero-centred odd pair, the zero-to-pi pair, the reciprocal misfits.
Why $\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ is forced for sine inverse
To invert sine we need one stretch meeting two demands at once.
D1 one-to-one: sine strictly monotonic there, each output used once.
D2 onto: the stretch must produce every value in $[-1,1]$.
On $\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ sine rises strictly from $-1$ to $+1$: both demands met.

board_events.caption: The smallest, most central monotonic window

board_events.text: It is also the stretch nearest the origin, which is why convention crowns it 'principal'.
Same rule everywhere: cosine gets $[0,\pi]$ (strictly falling), tangent the open $\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$.
Why sec drops half-pi and cosec drops zero
Secant is one over cosine. Borrow cosine's cage $[0,\pi]$.
At $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, cosine is zero, so secant is one over zero: undefined. No input can map there.
Delete that single point: sec's branch is $[0,\pi]$ minus $\left\{\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right\}$.
Cosecant is one over sine. Borrow sine's cage, then delete zero, where sine is zero.

segments.text: <curious>Here is a question that sounds trivial but really isn't. Which angle has a sine of one half? Your first instinct says thirty degrees, that is pi over six.

But hold on. One hundred fifty degrees also has a sine of one half. So does three hundred ninety degrees, and five hundred ten degrees, and minus three hundred thirty degrees, and infinitely many more.
This is the whole problem in one sentence. The sine function carries many different angles to the very same value. We say it is many to one.

And that property is fatal for inversion. An inverse function must hand back exactly one answer. A machine that, fed one half, spits out pi over six or five pi over six or thirteen pi over six is simply not a function at all.
Picture the sine curve. Draw a horizontal line at height one half, and watch it slice through the curve again and again and again. One value, endlessly many angles crossing it.

So here is the cure. We shrink sine's domain down to a single stretch on which it is one to one, each output used exactly once, and on which it still sweeps its whole range from minus one up to plus one.
The stretch the world has agreed on runs from minus pi over two to pi over two. Across it, sine climbs steadily and hits every value exactly once. Now our question has one honest answer, pi over six.
<whisper>And that chosen stretch has a name. It is called the principal value branch. Think of it as the single official platform where the answer is allowed to stand.
Before we compute anything, lock in two facts. Nearly every mark in this chapter turns on them.
Fact one. The principal value branch is a choice, but a fixed one. We agreed on it, and we never quietly change it mid problem.

There are infinitely many one to one stretches we could have picked. The source even mentions a perfectly valid non principal branch of cosine, like two pi to three pi. But the world crowns one canonical branch per function, so that sine inverse of one half means the very same thing in Wichita and in Kota.
<excited>Fact two, and this is the big one. The output of an inverse trig function is an angle, and that angle is trapped inside its branch. Always.

So the moment you write sine inverse of anything equals two pi over three, you have already made an error. Because two pi over three is one hundred twenty degrees, and that sits outside the cage from minus pi over two to pi over two.
Picture the branch as a cage with two solid walls. Whatever you feed in, the answer can rattle around inside, but it can never escape those walls.
Each of the six trig functions gets its own designated cage, and the shape of that cage is decided purely by symmetry.

Here is the shape rule in one breath. Sine and tangent hug zero, their cages are centred on it. Cosine and cotangent climb from zero up to pi. And secant and cosecant borrow those two cages, then delete one forbidden point each.
Here is the table the whole chapter leans on. Six inverse functions, each with a domain of legal inputs and a branch that cages its output.
Read every row the same way. y equals f inverse of x means y is the unique angle, living inside the branch b, whose f equals x. That is the entire definition.
Look at the table as a picture. On the left, the domain, the inputs you are allowed to feed in. On the right, the branch, the cage where the answer angle must live.

Notice the domains. Sine inverse and cosine inverse only accept inputs between minus one and one, because sine and cosine themselves never leave that range. But tangent inverse and cotangent inverse accept every real number.

Secant inverse and cosecant inverse are stricter. They need the absolute value of x to be at least one. That is because a reciprocal can never land strictly between minus one and one, so those inputs are simply illegal.
Watch the endpoints carefully. Tangent's cage is open at plus and minus pi over two, and cotangent's is open at zero and pi, because the function blows up exactly there.

And the reciprocal misfits punch a hole. Secant inverse drops pi over two, where cosine is zero. Cosecant inverse drops zero, where sine is zero. That deleted point is the tell that identifies which cage you are looking at.

So do not memorise eighteen loose facts. Memorise three patterns. The zero centred odd pair, sine and tangent. The zero to pi pair, cosine and cotangent. And the reciprocal misfits, secant and cosecant.
The branches are not handed down arbitrarily. They are forced, and once you see why, you never have to memorise them blind again.
To invert sine, we hunt for one stretch of the x axis that satisfies two demands at the very same time.
Demand one is that sine must be one to one there, meaning strictly monotonic, so each output value is used exactly once and inversion is even possible.
Demand two is that the stretch must be onto the full range. It has to produce every value between minus one and one, or the inverse would be undefined for some perfectly legal input.
Now check the interval from minus pi over two to pi over two. On it, sine increases strictly, climbing from minus one all the way to plus one. Both demands satisfied at once.
Picture it. This is the smallest, most central window on which sine both rises without repeating and sweeps its entire range. Nothing is wasted, nothing is missed.
It is also the stretch closest to the origin. That closeness is exactly why convention crowns it the principal branch, rather than some far away window that also happens to work.

And the identical reasoning gives every other branch. Cosine gets zero to pi, where it falls strictly from plus one to minus one. Tangent gets the open interval minus pi over two to pi over two. Same rule, pick the origin nearest monotonic window that sweeps the whole range.
The trickiest two cages belong to secant and cosecant. But their story is short once you see they are just reciprocals wearing a disguise.
Start with secant. Secant is one over cosine. So to build its cage, we simply borrow cosine's branch, the interval from zero to pi.
But there is a snag. At pi over two, cosine equals zero. So secant would be one over zero, which is undefined. No input value x can ever map to pi over two.
The fix is surgical. We delete that single point. Secant inverse's branch is zero to pi, minus the point pi over two. One clean hole.
Cosecant follows the identical logic. Cosecant is one over sine, so it borrows sine's branch. Then it deletes zero, because sine is zero there and the reciprocal blows up.
Here is the picture. Each function takes the parent cage as a solid bar, then punches out exactly one point where the reciprocal explodes. Secant loses pi over two, cosecant loses zero.
There is one more consequence worth naming. Their domains exclude the open interval from minus one to one entirely, because a reciprocal can never sit strictly between minus one and one.
So that is the whole secant and cosecant story. The cosine based one, secant, drops half pi. The sine based one, cosecant, drops zero. Remember which parent, and the deleted point follows.

segments.text: <curious>Ek sawaal jo trivial lagta hai, but hai nahi. Kis angle ka sine one half hota hai? Pehla instinct kehta hai thirty degrees, yaani pi over six.
Lekin ruko. One hundred fifty degrees ka sine bhi one half hai. Aur three hundred ninety degrees, five hundred ten degrees, minus three hundred thirty degrees, aur infinitely many aur bhi.
Yahi toh poori problem hai ek line mein. Sine function bahut saare alag alag angles ko same value par bhej deta hai. Ise hum kehte hain many to one.

Aur yeh property inversion ke liye fatal hai. Ek inverse function ko exactly ek hi answer dena hota hai. Jo machine one half daalne par pi over six ya five pi over six ya thirteen pi over six bolne lage, woh function hai hi nahi.
Sine curve ko imagine karo. Height one half par ek horizontal line kheencho, aur dekho woh curve ko baar baar cut karti hai. Ek value, aur endless angles use cross karte hue.
Toh ilaaj yeh hai. Hum sine ka domain chota kar dete hain ek aise stretch tak jahaan woh one to one ho, har output sirf ek baar use ho, aur jo poora range minus one se plus one tak cover kare.

Jis stretch par duniya agree karti hai woh chalta hai minus pi over two se pi over two tak. Is par sine steadily climb karta hai aur har value ko exactly ek baar hit karta hai. Ab hamare sawaal ka ek honest answer hai, pi over six.
<whisper>Aur us chosen stretch ka ek naam hai. Ise kehte hain principal value branch. Ise samjho ek official platform jahaan answer ko khade hone ki permission milti hai.
Kuch bhi compute karne se pehle, do facts lock kar lo. Is chapter ke lagbhag saare marks inhi par tikte hain.
Fact one. Principal value branch ek choice hai, lekin ek fixed choice. Humne ise agree kiya hai, aur beech problem mein chupke se change nahi karte.

Infinitely many one to one stretches the jinhe hum choose kar sakte the. Source toh cosine ka ek valid non principal branch bhi mention karta hai, jaise two pi se three pi. Lekin duniya har function ke liye ek canonical branch crown karti hai, taaki sine inverse of one half ka matlab Wichita mein aur Kota mein bilkul same rahe.
<excited>Fact two, aur yeh sabse bada hai. Inverse trig function ka output ek angle hota hai, aur woh angle apne branch ke andar trapped rehta hai. Hamesha.

Toh jis pal aap likhte ho sine inverse of anything equals two pi over three, wahi galti ho gayi. Kyunki two pi over three ka matlab one hundred twenty degrees, aur woh cage se bahar hai, minus pi over two se pi over two ke bahar.
Branch ko ek cage samjho jiski do solid walls hain. Jo bhi feed karo, answer andar bounce kar sakta hai, lekin un walls ke bahar kabhi nahi ja sakta.
Cheh trig functions mein se har ek ko apna designated cage milta hai, aur us cage ki shape sirf symmetry se decide hoti hai.

Shape rule ek saans mein. Sine aur tangent zero ko hug karte hain, unke cages usi par centred hain. Cosine aur cotangent zero se pi tak climb karte hain. Aur secant aur cosecant un dono cages ko borrow karte hain, phir ek ek forbidden point delete kar dete hain.
Yeh rahi woh table jis par poora chapter tika hai. Cheh inverse functions, har ek ka ek domain of legal inputs, aur ek branch jo uske output ko cage karta hai.
Har row ko ek hi tareeke se padho. y equals f inverse of x ka matlab, y woh unique angle hai, jo branch b ke andar rehta hai, aur jiska f equals x. Bas yahi poori definition hai.
Table ko ek picture ki tarah dekho. Left par domain, woh inputs jo aap feed kar sakte ho. Right par branch, woh cage jahaan answer angle ko rehna hi hai.

Domains par dhyaan do. Sine inverse aur cosine inverse sirf minus one se one ke beech ke inputs lete hain, kyunki sine aur cosine khud us range ke bahar jaate hi nahi. Lekin tangent inverse aur cotangent inverse har real number accept karte hain.

Secant inverse aur cosecant inverse zyada strict hain. Inhe chahiye ki x ki absolute value at least one ho. Kyunki ek reciprocal kabhi minus one aur one ke strictly beech land nahi karta, toh woh inputs simply illegal hain.
Endpoints ko dhyaan se dekho. Tangent ka cage plus aur minus pi over two par open hai, aur cotangent ka zero aur pi par open hai, kyunki function theek wahi blow up karta hai.

Aur reciprocal misfits ek hole punch karte hain. Secant inverse pi over two drop karta hai, jahaan cosine zero hai. Cosecant inverse zero drop karta hai, jahaan sine zero hai. Wahi deleted point tell hai jo batata hai aap kaunsa cage dekh rahe ho.
Toh atharah loose facts mat ratto. Teen patterns ratto. Zero centred odd pair, sine aur tangent. Zero to pi pair, cosine aur cotangent. Aur reciprocal misfits, secant aur cosecant.
Branches arbitrarily nahi thope gaye. Woh forced hain, aur ek baar aap dekh lo kyun, phir kabhi blindly ratna nahi padega.
Sine ko invert karne ke liye, hum x axis ka ek aisa stretch dhoondte hain jo do demands ko ek hi time par satisfy kare.
Demand one, sine wahaan one to one hona chahiye, matlab strictly monotonic, taaki har output value exactly ek baar use ho aur inversion possible bhi ho.
Demand two, woh stretch full range par onto hona chahiye. Use minus one se one ke beech ki har value produce karni hai, warna kisi perfectly legal input ke liye inverse undefined ho jaayega.
Ab check karo interval minus pi over two se pi over two. Is par sine strictly increase karta hai, minus one se seedha plus one tak climb karta hai. Dono demands ek saath satisfied.
Ise imagine karo. Yeh sabse chota, sabse central window hai jis par sine repeat kiye bina rise karta hai aur apna poora range sweep karta hai. Na kuch waste, na kuch miss.
Yeh origin ke sabse paas wala stretch bhi hai. Yahi closeness reason hai ki convention ise principal branch crown karti hai, kisi door wale window ke bajaye jo waise toh kaam kar bhi jaata.

board_events.text: CBSE level: find the principal values
Rule: find the angle inside the branch whose trig value matches.
Branch check: every answer sits inside its cage.
We never 'undo' blindly. We hunt the in-branch angle whose value matches.
CUET speed + JEE Main range-fold
Which is the branch of cosec inverse? Scan for sine's cage minus a point.
The deleted point is the tell: sec drops half-pi, cosec drops zero.
JEE Main: evaluate $\sin^{-1}\!\left(\sin\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)$. Branch $\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$; $\tfrac{2\pi}{3}$ is outside.
JEE Advanced: three moves
Evaluate $\tan^{-1}\!\left(\tan\tfrac{3\pi}{4}\right)$. Branch open $\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$; $\tfrac{3\pi}{4}$ is outside.
Express $\sin^{-1}(\sin x)$ for $x \in \left[\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{3\pi}{2}\right]$ using $\sin x = \sin(\pi - x)$.
Endpoints: at $x=\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, $\pi-x=\tfrac{\pi}{2}$; at $x=\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$, $\pi-x=-\tfrac{\pi}{2}$: both inside.
Does secant inverse of one half exist? Run the domain check first.
Since $\left|\tfrac{1}{2}\right| \lt 1$ and $|\sec\theta| \ge 1$ always, sec inverse of one half does NOT exist.

Two: answering outside the branch. Check the branch first, fold if needed.

Four: sec-cosec confusion. Sec is cosine-based (drops half-pi); cosec is sine-based (drops zero).
Five: mode mismatch. Higher exams want radians: don't leave $30^\circ$ when the key wants $\tfrac{\pi}{6}$.
Ritual: write the branch, ask 'is theta inside?', if not, fold. Then branch-check the answer.

segments.text: Every inverse trig answer comes with two free sanity checks, the way physics gives you dimensional analysis. Use them every single time.

The domain check comes first, before you compute anything. Is x a legal input at all? And the branch check comes last. Does your output angle y actually lie inside the branch b? If not, you have made an error, guaranteed.
Now the folding tools. The first identity, sine of pi minus theta equals sine theta. This lets you swap an angle for a partner with the same sine.
The second, cosine of two pi minus theta equals cosine of minus theta equals cosine theta. Cosine is even, so this reflection preserves its value.
The third, tangent of theta plus or minus pi equals tangent theta. Tangent simply repeats every pi, so you can shift by pi freely.

Here is the recipe that neutralises the single most common trap in this chapter. When you meet f inverse of f of theta, do three things. Read the branch of the outer inverse. Use a value preserving identity to replace the inner angle by an equivalent one that sits inside that branch. Then the inverse returns that in branch angle directly.

Watch it work. Evaluate cosine inverse of cosine of seven pi over six. The branch is zero to pi. Seven pi over six is two hundred ten degrees, outside it. Fold, cosine of seven pi over six equals cosine of five pi over six, and five pi over six is inside the branch. So the answer is five pi over six, not seven pi over six.
See it on the number line. Seven pi over six sits outside the green band. The fold identity carries it to five pi over six, which lands safely inside. Fold first, then read off the answer.
Let us do the classic C B S E one to two mark question, find the principal values, three parts. The method is the same each time.
The rule is simple. In each part, find the one angle sitting inside the correct branch whose trig value matches the input. That angle is the principal value.

Part a, sine inverse of minus one half. The branch is minus pi over two to pi over two. We need an angle in there whose sine is minus one half. Sine of minus pi over six is minus one half, and minus pi over six lives inside the branch.
So sine inverse of minus one half equals minus pi over six. Clean.
Part b, cosine inverse of root three over two. The branch here is zero to pi. Cosine of pi over six is root three over two, and pi over six is inside zero to pi. So the answer is pi over six.
Part c, tangent inverse of one. Tangent of pi over four is one, and pi over four sits inside the open branch. So tangent inverse of one equals pi over four.
Now run the branch check on all three. Minus pi over six, pi over six, pi over four. Every single answer sits safely inside its own cage. Tick.
Notice the mindset throughout. We never blindly undo the trig function. We hunt for the in branch angle whose value matches the input. That habit is what keeps you inside the cage.
Now two exam styles back to back. First a C U E T speed trap, then the headline J E E Main fold.
The C U E T one liner asks, which of these is the principal value branch of cosecant inverse? Do not compute. Just scan for sine's cage with a single point removed.

Cosecant inverse borrows sine's branch, minus pi over two to pi over two, and deletes the forbidden point where sine is zero, namely zero itself. So the branch is minus pi over two to pi over two, minus the point zero.
That deleted point is the whole tell. Secant drops half pi, cosecant drops zero. The distractor options are the tangent branch, the secant branch, or the version that forgot to delete zero.

Now the J E E Main favourite. Evaluate sine inverse of sine of two pi over three. The branch is minus pi over two to pi over two. Two pi over three is one hundred twenty degrees, which is outside. So we must fold, we cannot just cancel.

Fold with sine of pi minus theta equals sine theta. Sine of two pi over three equals sine of pi minus two pi over three, which is sine of pi over three. And pi over three is inside the branch. So the answer is pi over three, not two pi over three.
The same recipe handles cosine inverse of cosine of seven pi over six. Branch zero to pi, seven pi over six outside, fold to five pi over six inside. Answer, five pi over six.

And one with degrees. Cosine inverse of cosine of minus six hundred eighty degrees. Cosine is even, so drop the sign. Six hundred eighty is seven hundred twenty minus forty, so its cosine equals cosine of forty degrees, and forty degrees is inside zero to one hundred eighty. So the answer is forty degrees, that is two pi over nine.
Now the J E E Advanced flavour, three moves that stack the branch idea into harder shapes.

Move one, evaluate tangent inverse of tangent of three pi over four. The tangent inverse branch is the open interval minus pi over two to pi over two. Three pi over four is one hundred thirty five degrees, outside it. So fold.

Fold using tangent of theta minus pi equals tangent theta. Tangent of three pi over four equals tangent of three pi over four minus pi, which is tangent of minus pi over four. And minus pi over four is inside the open branch. So the answer is minus pi over four.

Move two is deeper. Express sine inverse of sine x as a simple formula for every x from pi over two to three pi over two. On this whole interval x sits outside the sine branch, so we fold with sine x equals sine of pi minus x.
And here is the key claim. On this interval, sine inverse of sine x equals pi minus x. Not x, but pi minus x.

Prove it at the endpoints. At x equals pi over two, pi minus x is pi over two, inside. At x equals three pi over two, pi minus x is minus pi over two, inside. And pi minus x runs smoothly through the branch in between. So pi minus x is the honest answer across the whole interval.
Move three, does secant inverse of one half exist? Before any angle hunting, run the domain check.

Secant inverse requires the absolute value of the input to be at least one. But the absolute value of one half is less than one. And the secant of any real angle always has absolute value at least one. So there is no angle whose secant is one half. Secant inverse of one half simply does not exist.
Let us close Part one with the five ways students bleed easy marks here, and the one ritual that stops all of them.
Loss one, the cardinal sin. Reading sine inverse of x as one over sine x. That minus one is an inverse function marker, not a reciprocal power.

Keep them separate. Sine inverse of x is an angle. One over sine x is cosecant x, a plain ratio. Two completely different objects. If you actually want the reciprocal, write sine x in brackets, then minus one.

Loss two, answering outside the branch, the range folding failure. Writing sine inverse of sine of two pi over three as two pi over three. The cancel identity holds only when the angle is already inside the branch. So always check the branch first, and fold if you must.

Loss three, domain blindness. Sine inverse of two, secant inverse of zero point seven, cosecant inverse of zero, all undefined. Run the domain check before computing anything, because an answer to an undefined expression scores a flat zero.

Loss four, secant and cosecant confusion, the classic C U E T banana skin. Secant is cosine based and drops half pi. Cosecant is sine based and drops zero. Mixing them, or forgetting the deletion, is exactly what the paper is testing.

Loss five, mode mismatch. Higher exams state principal values in radians. Do not leave a board answer as thirty degrees when the marking key wants pi over six, and read the question for which one it wants.

<whisper>And here is the ritual that makes you almost impossible to trick. For any f inverse of f of theta, do three things every time. Write the branch. Ask, is theta inside it? If not, fold. Then run the free branch check on your final answer. That two second habit converts the highest frequency trap in this chapter into a guaranteed mark.

board_events.text: One rule generates the whole negative-argument table
In Part 1 each inverse lived in a cage. Now feed the cage a transformed input, $-x$.
Sine, tangent, cosecant have branches centred on $0$, symmetric about the origin.
Cosine, secant, cotangent have branches on $[0,\pi]$, sitting entirely on the positive side.
Zero-centred branch absorbs a sign flip: $f^{-1}(-x) = -f^{-1}(x)$. These are ODD.
$[0,\pi]$ branch can't go negative, so it reflects: $f^{-1}(-x) = \pi - f^{-1}(x)$. The $\pi-$ functions.

board_events.text: Memorise the rule, not the six rows: odd for the zero-centred trio, $\pi-$ for the $[0,\pi]$ trio.
Why exactly two responses?
Negating the input is the instruction: 'now stand at your mirror position.'
If your zone straddles zero (sine's branch), your mirror image is still inside: swap sides, sign flipped.
If your zone runs from the wall at $0$ to the wall at $\pi$ (cosine's branch), the naive mirror lands behind a wall: illegal.
So you reflect about the room's centre $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, landing at $\pi$ minus your spot: still legal.
Complementary identities come from the oldest fact: $\sin\theta = \cos\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)$, so the two angles sum to $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$.
Reciprocal identities are even simpler: cosec is the reciprocal of sin, so inverting a reciprocal returns the co-function.
Hold one sentence: odd for the zero-centred trio, $\pi-$ for the $[0,\pi]$ trio.
Three derivations, all forced by the branch
Odd: let $\sin^{-1}x = y$, so $\sin y = x$, with $y\in\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$.
$\pi-$: let $\cos^{-1}x = y$, $y\in[0,\pi]$. Naive $-y$ is illegal; use $\cos(\pi-y) = -\cos y = -x$.
Complementary: with $\sin^{-1}x = y$, the co-relation $\cos\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}-y\right) = \sin y = x$ holds, and $\tfrac{\pi}{2}-y\in[0,\pi]$.
The branch check isn't a formality: it is exactly what lands the partner angle in the right cage.
The highest-value trap: $\tan^{-1}\tfrac{1}{x}$
Let $\cot^{-1}x = y$, so $\cot y = x$ with $y\in(0,\pi)$, hence $\tan y = \tfrac{1}{x}$.
If $x \gt 0$: then $y\in\left(0,\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, inside tan inverse's cage.
If $x \lt 0$: then $y\in\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2},\pi\right)$, OUTSIDE the cage. The in-cage angle is $y-\pi$.

segments.text: In Part one every inverse function lived inside a cage, its principal value branch. Now we do something new. We feed the cage a transformed input, a negation, minus x.
<curious>And here is the remarkable thing. The negation does not produce messy new angles. It produces the same family of angles, shifted or reflected in one of exactly two ways.
The split is set by branch shape. Sine, tangent and cosecant have branches centred on zero, symmetric about the origin.
Cosine, secant and cotangent are different. Their branches run from zero up to pi, sitting entirely on the positive side.
That one geometric difference decides everything. A branch centred on zero can absorb a sign flip and stay inside itself. Negate the input, negate the answer. So sine, tangent and cosecant are odd.

But a branch trapped on zero to pi can never go negative. A negative answer would jump straight out of the cage. So instead the answer reflects across the midpoint pi over two, landing at pi minus the original. These are the pi minus functions.

See it side by side. On the left, the zero centred branch, plus theta and minus theta both sit safely inside. On the right, the zero to pi branch, the naive mirror lands outside, so we reflect through the centre instead.
So do not memorise six separate rows. Memorise one rule. Odd for the zero centred trio, pi minus for the zero to pi trio.
Why exactly two responses, and not five? Here is the intuition, in classroom terms.
Imagine a row of students standing on a number line. Negate the input is just the instruction, now stand at your mirror position, on the other side of zero.
If your allowed standing zone straddles zero, that is sine's branch, then your mirror image is still inside the zone. You simply swap to the other side, with your sign flipped. That is the odd rule.
But if your allowed zone runs from the wall at zero to the wall at pi, that is cosine's branch, then your naive mirror image would land behind the wall at zero. Illegal, out of bounds.

So instead you reflect about the centre of the room, pi over two, and you land at pi minus your original spot, still legally inside. Same instruction, two different legal responses, decided entirely by where your room sits.
The complementary identities come from the oldest trig fact of all. Sine of theta equals cosine of pi over two minus theta. Inverted, that says the two angles must add up to pi over two.
And the reciprocal identities are even more direct. Cosecant is the reciprocal of sine, so inverting a reciprocal simply returns the co function, with a domain caveat we will pin down next.
None of this needs raw memorisation if you hold one sentence. Odd for the zero centred trio, pi minus for the zero to pi trio. Everything in this subtopic is that one sentence, written out.
Now let us actually derive the three laws, so you never have to trust them blind. Each one is forced by the branch.
Start with the odd law. Let sine inverse of x equal y, so sine of y is x, with y living in minus pi over two to pi over two.

Now take sine of minus y. That equals minus sine y, which is minus x. And crucially, minus y is still inside the branch, because the branch is symmetric about zero. So minus y qualifies as the principal value of sine inverse of minus x. Sine inverse of minus x equals minus sine inverse of x. The same argument runs verbatim for tangent and cosecant.

Now the pi minus law. Let cosine inverse of x equal y, with y in zero to pi. Try the naive move, minus y. But minus y is not in zero to pi, illegal. Instead use cosine of pi minus y, which equals minus cosine y, which is minus x.

And check the cage. Since y is in zero to pi, pi minus y is also in zero to pi. Legal. So pi minus y is the principal value of cosine inverse of minus x. Cosine inverse of minus x equals pi minus cosine inverse of x.

Finally the complementary law. With sine inverse of x equal to y, the co relation says cosine of pi over two minus y equals sine y, which is x. And we check, pi over two minus y does lie inside cosine's cage, zero to pi.
So cosine inverse of x equals pi over two minus y. Add the two, sine inverse of x plus cosine inverse of x equals y plus pi over two minus y, which is pi over two. The identity falls out cleanly.
Notice the branch check appearing in every derivation. It is not a formality. It is exactly the step that guarantees the partner angle lands in the right cage.

Let cotangent inverse of x equal y, so cotangent of y is x, with y in the open interval zero to pi. Take reciprocals, and tangent of y is one over x.

segments.text: Here is the full identity set for this subtopic, gathered in one place. Two families, reciprocal and negative argument.

Family one, the reciprocal identities. Sine inverse of one over x equals cosecant inverse of x, and cosine inverse of one over x equals secant inverse of x. Both require the absolute value of x to be at least one, so that one over x is small enough to be a legal input.
The tangent reciprocal is the sign sensitive one. Tangent inverse of one over x equals cotangent inverse of x, but only for positive x. For negative x you subtract pi.
Family two is the negative argument set, and it splits cleanly along the branch line. First the odd trio.
For the zero centred branch, sine, tangent and cosecant, the sign simply flips. Sine inverse of minus x is minus sine inverse of x, and the same for tangent and cosecant.
Now the pi minus trio. These have branches on zero to pi.
For cosine, secant and cotangent, a negative argument reflects through pi over two. Cosine inverse of minus x equals pi minus cosine inverse of x, and identically for secant and cotangent.
One warning on all of these. Every identity is legal only on its own function's domain. Quote it outside that domain and the answer scores a flat zero, however clean the algebra looks.
The third family is the complementary identities, and they are the friendliest of the lot. Each co pair adds up to a right angle.
Sine inverse of x plus cosine inverse of x equals pi over two, valid for every x from minus one to one.
Tangent inverse of x plus cotangent inverse of x equals pi over two, and this one holds for every real number x.
Cosecant inverse of x plus secant inverse of x equals pi over two, valid whenever the absolute value of x is at least one.
Here is the fact students most often break. The complementary law is sign agnostic. It holds for every legal x, positive or negative alike. Do not try to correct it for negative x.
Picture why. Sine inverse of x and cosine inverse of x are two complementary angles. Placed together, they fill exactly one right angle, pi over two. That is the whole identity in one image.
Carry two reflexes from Part one. Reflex one, the domain gate. Apply sine inverse plus cosine inverse at x equals two and you have written nonsense, because neither term even exists there.
Reflex two, branch sanity. After you apply any pi minus step, the answer must still sit inside zero to pi. If a pi minus result comes out negative, you accidentally used the odd form.
Let us apply the identities on a C B S E level question, three parts, each one testing a different family.
Part a, sine inverse of minus one half. Sine inverse is odd, so pull the sign straight out. Minus sine inverse of one half, which is minus pi over six. Done in one line.
Part b tests whether you really understood the split. Cosine is not odd, so you must use the pi minus form, never a sign flip.
So cosine inverse of minus root three over two equals pi minus cosine inverse of root three over two, which is pi minus pi over six, giving five pi over six.
This is where marks vanish. Writing minus pi over six here is the classic error. Five pi over six is the branch legal answer, because it sits inside zero to pi, while minus pi over six does not.
Part c, a quick verification of the complementary law at x equals one half.
Sine inverse of one half is pi over six, cosine inverse of one half is pi over three. Add them, pi over six plus pi over three is pi over two. The law checks out perfectly.
Take away one reflex from all three. The instant you see a negative argument sitting on cosine, secant or cotangent, your hand should write pi minus before you compute anything else.
Two exam styles now. First a C U E T speed one liner, then a J E E Main problem lifted straight from N C E R T.
Evaluate cotangent inverse of minus root three. The instant you see cotangent inverse of a negative, remember it is a pi minus function. Its branch is zero to pi, so it is never negative.
So cotangent inverse of minus root three equals pi minus cotangent inverse of root three, which is pi minus pi over six, giving five pi over six.
The trap answer is minus pi over six. That is the odd function reflex applied by mistake to a pi minus function. Do not fall for it.
Now the J E E Main favourite, an actual N C E R T objective question. Evaluate tangent inverse of root three minus cotangent inverse of minus root three.
The first term, tangent inverse of root three, is pi over three. The second term we just found, cotangent inverse of minus root three is five pi over six, using the pi minus form.
So the expression is pi over three minus five pi over six. Put over a common denominator, two pi over six minus five pi over six, which is minus three pi over six, that is minus pi over two.
The trap answer zero comes from wrongly treating cotangent inverse as odd. Handle the negative correctly with pi minus, and the true value is minus pi over two.

board_events.text: JEE Advanced: the famous piecewise result
Simplify $\tan^{-1}x + \tan^{-1}\tfrac{1}{x}$ for all real $x\neq 0$. Use the sign-sensitive reciprocal identity.
Case $x \gt 0$: here $\tan^{-1}\tfrac{1}{x} = \cot^{-1}x$, and $\tan^{-1}x + \cot^{-1}x = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$.
Case $x \lt 0$: here $\tan^{-1}\tfrac{1}{x} = \cot^{-1}x - \pi$, so the sum drops by $\pi$.
The whole difficulty is the single $-\pi$ the reciprocal identity hides for $x \lt 0$.
Four losses + one reflex
One (cardinal sin): 'all six identities are odd.' Only sin, tan, cosec flip sign.
Anchor it: a $[0,\pi]$ cage can never output a negative angle, so it cannot be odd.
Two: reciprocal sign-blindness. $\tan^{-1}\tfrac{1}{x} = \cot^{-1}x$ only for $x \gt 0$; else subtract $\pi$.
Three: ignoring domain gates. $\sin^{-1}x + \cos^{-1}x = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$ needs $|x|\le 1$; the reciprocal pair needs $|x|\ge 1$.
Four: 'correcting' the complementary law for negative $x$. It is sign-agnostic, so leave it alone.
The reflex: negative argument on cos, sec, or cot $\Rightarrow$ write '$\pi-$' first, evaluate second.
Pair that reflex with the Part 1 branch-check and this whole family becomes free marks.
Two functions in, one function out
In Part 2 we transformed a single inverse. Now we combine two: add $\tan^{-1}x$ and $\tan^{-1}y$.
The engine is the ordinary addition formula, run backwards. Name the angles $A$ and $B$.
Tempting to write $A+B = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{x+y}{1-xy}$: right, as long as $A+B$ stays in the cage $\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$.
If $x,y$ both large positive ($xy \gt 1$), the sum overshoots $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$: add $\pi$. Both large negative: subtract $\pi$.

board_events.text: Multiple-angle identities are the same story with $y=x$: an addition or triple formula read backwards, fenced by a domain.
Why three cases, not one
Let $A=\tan^{-1}x$, $B=\tan^{-1}y$, so $A,B\in\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ and $\tan(A+B)=\dfrac{x+y}{1-xy}$.
But $A+B$ ranges over $(-\pi,\pi)$: wider than the tan cage. Hence three cases.
The $\pm\pi$ is purely the branch correction: the same folding idea as Part 1.
This is why 'compute $xy$ first' is the automatic opening move on any arctangent sum.

segments.text: Now the famous J E E Advanced result. Simplify tangent inverse of x plus tangent inverse of one over x, for every real x except zero. State the answer piecewise.
The key is the sign sensitive reciprocal identity from earlier, combined with the complementary law that tangent inverse plus cotangent inverse is pi over two.

Take the positive case first. For x greater than zero, tangent inverse of one over x equals cotangent inverse of x. So the sum becomes tangent inverse of x plus cotangent inverse of x, which is exactly the complementary law.
So for positive x, the whole expression is pi over two. Clean and constant.
Now the negative case, where the hidden minus pi appears. For x less than zero, tangent inverse of one over x equals cotangent inverse of x minus pi. So the sum picks up an extra minus pi.
That gives pi over two minus pi, which is minus pi over two. So for negative x, the answer is minus pi over two, not pi over two.
Sanity check both cases at the units. At x equals one, pi over four plus pi over four is pi over two. At x equals minus one, minus pi over four minus pi over four is minus pi over two. Both match.
So the whole difficulty of this famous result is the single minus pi that the reciprocal identity quietly hides for negative x. See that, and the problem is trivial.
Let us close Part two with the four ways students lose marks here, and the one reflex that neutralises most of them.
Loss one, the cardinal sin. Believing all six identities are odd. They are not. Only sine, tangent and cosecant flip the sign.
Anchor the truth to the geometry. A zero to pi cage can never output a negative angle, so those three functions simply cannot be odd. Cosine, secant and cotangent must use pi minus.

Loss two, reciprocal sign blindness. Tangent inverse of one over x equals cotangent inverse of x only for positive x. For negative x you must subtract pi. Always check the sign before quoting this one.

Loss three, ignoring the domain gates. Sine inverse plus cosine inverse equals pi over two needs the absolute value of x at most one. The reciprocal pair needs the absolute value at least one. Quote an identity outside its domain and it is an automatic zero.
Loss four, correcting the complementary law for negative x. Students sometimes think a negative input needs a fix and break a correct answer. The complementary law is sign agnostic. Leave it alone.
<whisper>And here is the reflex that ties it all together. A negative argument sitting on cosine, secant or cotangent means write pi minus first, evaluate second.
Pair that one reflex with the branch check from Part one, and this entire self map family turns into free, reliable marks.
In Part two, every identity transformed a single inverse function. Now we combine two of them. We add tangent inverse of x and tangent inverse of y, and ask what single inverse function comes out.
The engine is nothing new. It is the ordinary trigonometric addition formula, simply run backwards.
Name the two angles. Let A be tangent inverse of x and B be tangent inverse of y. They are just two ordinary angles.
You already know the tangent of A plus B. It is tangent A plus tangent B over one minus tangent A tangent B, which is x plus y over one minus x y.
So it is tempting to write A plus B equals tangent inverse of that fraction. And that is right, as long as A plus B has not escaped the tangent cage, minus pi over two to pi over two.

<curious>But here is the subtlety. If x and y are both large and positive, which happens exactly when x y exceeds one, their sum overshoots pi over two and lands outside the cage. Then you must add pi back. If both are large negative, the sum undershoots and you subtract pi.

See it on the axis. The formula hands you a raw value inside the cage. But the true A plus B sits outside, a full pi away. Adding pi is not a special rule to memorise. It is just the cage reasserting itself, exactly like the folding from Part one.

And the multiple angle identities are the very same story with y equal to x. Every one of them is an addition or a triple formula read backwards, fenced by a domain condition that keeps the doubled or tripled angle inside its cage.

Let A be tangent inverse of x and B be tangent inverse of y. Each lives in the open cage minus pi over two to pi over two, and the tangent of their sum is x plus y over one minus x y.

Case three, x y greater than one with both negative. Symmetrically the sum lands between minus pi and minus pi over two, below the cage, so subtract pi.

sections.title: Arctangent sum and difference & related topics

board_events.text: The arctangent sum: compute $xy$ first
One number, $xy$, decides which line you are on.
Difference has a PLUS in the denominator, opposite of the sum. Mixing them is endemic.
All of these come from the addition formula backwards; the $\pm\pi$ is the branch correction.
Doubling: three faces of $2\tan^{-1}x$
Same left side, three different domain fences: each form guards its own branch.
Read the fence before you read the formula: the fence is where the marks live.
Tripling + arcsine/arccosine sums
When the stated condition fails, a $\pm\pi$ or $2\pi-$ correction applies: same cage logic.
These arcsine and arccosine sums are the condition-heavy JEE Advanced tools; handle the domain with care.
Validity check: after combining, the result must lie in the combined function's branch.
CBSE proof + CUET double-angle
Prove $\tan^{-1}\tfrac{1}{2} + \tan^{-1}\tfrac{1}{3} = \tfrac{\pi}{4}$. First compute $xy$.
CUET: write $2\tan^{-1}\tfrac{1}{3}$ as a single $\tan^{-1}$. Here $|x|=\tfrac{1}{3} \lt 1$.
Compute $xy$ first is the reflex; $\tfrac{1}{6} \lt 1$ told us to skip the $\pi$ correction.
Both are clean because the product stayed below one: no cage overshoot.

segments.text: Here is the arctangent sum, gathered as three lines, plus the difference. And the opening move is always the same, compute x y first.
Line one, x y less than one. The sum is simply tangent inverse of x plus y over one minus x y. No correction at all.
Line two, x y greater than one with both x and y positive. Same fraction, but you add pi in front. This is the case exams punish most.
Line three, x y greater than one with both x and y negative. Same fraction, but you subtract pi.
So one single number, the product x y, decides which of these three lines you are standing on. Never touch the formula before you know it.
Now the difference. Tangent inverse of x minus tangent inverse of y equals tangent inverse of x minus y over one plus x y, valid when x y is greater than minus one.
Look carefully at that denominator. The difference has a plus sign in the denominator, the exact opposite of the minus in the sum. Mixing up these two signs is endemic, so anchor it now.
All of these come straight from the ordinary addition formula, read backwards. And the plus or minus pi you saw is nothing exotic. It is just the branch correction.
Now the doubling identities. The headline is that two tangent inverse of x wears three different faces, and each face carries its own domain fence.
Face one, two tangent inverse of x equals tangent inverse of two x over one minus x squared, valid when the absolute value of x is less than one.
Face two, the same left side equals sine inverse of two x over one plus x squared, valid when the absolute value of x is at most one.
Face three, the same left side equals cosine inverse of one minus x squared over one plus x squared, valid only for x at least zero.
Look at what just happened. Identical left side, three genuinely different fences. Each form guards a different branch, so the legal window shifts with the form you pick.
Two more doubles. Two sine inverse of x equals sine inverse of two x root one minus x squared, valid when the absolute value of x is at most one over root two.
And two cosine inverse of x equals cosine inverse of two x squared minus one, valid for x between zero and one.
The habit to build is simple. Read the fence before you read the formula. The formula is easy. The fence is exactly where the marks live.
The tripling identities and the arcsine and arccosine sums round out the toolkit. All of them are condition heavy.
Three sine inverse of x equals sine inverse of three x minus four x cubed, valid when x lies between minus one half and one half.
Three cosine inverse of x equals cosine inverse of four x cubed minus three x, valid when x lies between one half and one.
Now the arcsine sum. Sine inverse of x plus sine inverse of y equals sine inverse of x root one minus y squared plus y root one minus x squared, provided x squared plus y squared is at most one.
And the arccosine sum. Cosine inverse of x plus cosine inverse of y equals cosine inverse of x y minus root one minus x squared root one minus y squared, provided x plus y is at least zero.
When the stated condition fails, you do not throw the identity away. A plus or minus pi, or a two pi minus correction, steps in. It is the same cage logic as the arctangent sum.
These arcsine and arccosine sums are the condition heavy tools that JEE Advanced loves. Handle the domain with real care, because the condition is usually the whole point.
And keep the universal validity check running. After you combine, the result must lie inside the combined function's branch. If it does not, you dropped a correction term.
Two exam styles first, both in the clean, no correction regime. A C B S E proof, then a C U E T double angle.
Prove that tangent inverse of one half plus tangent inverse of one third equals pi over four. Before anything, compute the product x y.
The product is one half times one third, which is one sixth. That is less than one, so we are in the direct case with no pi correction.

Apply the formula. The numerator is one half plus one third, that is five sixths. The denominator is one minus one sixth, also five sixths. They cancel to one, and tangent inverse of one is pi over four. Proved.
Now the C U E T style. Write two tangent inverse of one third as a single tangent inverse. Here the absolute value of x is one third, comfortably less than one, so the tangent doubling form is legal.

Substitute. The numerator is two thirds. The denominator is one minus one ninth, which is eight ninths. Dividing, two thirds over eight ninths is three fourths. So the answer is tangent inverse of three fourths.
Notice the pattern in both. Compute x y first became the reflex. The value one sixth, being less than one, told us immediately to skip the pi correction.
Both stayed clean for one reason. The product stayed below one, so the combined angle never overshot the cage. No overshoot, no correction.

Four losses + the opening move

If $xy \gt 1$, decide the sign correction from the signs of $x,y$ before touching the formula.
Two: ignoring multiple-angle domains. $2\tan^{-1}x = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{2x}{1-x^2}$ only for $|x| \lt 1$.

Four: mis-reading telescoping. If your $\tan^{-1}a - \tan^{-1}b$ split doesn't cancel consecutively, it's wrong.

Every inverse is the parent, mirrored across $y=x$

segments.text: Now the J E E Main favourite, the case that separates the students who memorised from the students who understood.
Evaluate tangent inverse of two plus tangent inverse of three. Opening move, compute the product first.
The product is two times three, which is six. That is greater than one, and both terms are positive. So we are firmly in the plus pi case.

Apply the formula with the correction. Pi plus tangent inverse of two plus three over one minus six. The numerator is five, the denominator is minus five, so the fraction is minus one. That leaves pi plus tangent inverse of minus one.
Tangent inverse of minus one is minus pi over four. So we get pi minus pi over four, which is three pi over four.
The trap answer is minus pi over four, and it comes purely from forgetting the plus pi. A student who skips the correction lands there and loses the mark.
Now the beautiful part, a sanity check. Tangent inverse of two and tangent inverse of three each exceed pi over four, so their sum must exceed pi over two.
Only three pi over four exceeds pi over two. Minus pi over four does not even come close. The sanity check independently confirms that the correction was needed.
Finally, the canonical J E E Advanced telescoping series. It looks frightening and collapses to a single clean number.
Find the infinite sum of tangent inverse of one over one plus n plus n squared. The whole trick is to rewrite each term as a difference of two arctangents.
Here is the key algebra. One over one plus n plus n squared can be written as n plus one minus n, all over one plus n times n plus one. That is exactly the shape of the arctangent difference.
So the general term equals tangent inverse of n plus one minus tangent inverse of n. Every term is now a difference of two consecutive arctangents.
And that is what makes it telescope. Watch the middle terms. The positive part of one term cancels the negative part of the next, all the way down the chain.
So the partial sum up to capital N collapses. Almost everything cancels, leaving just tangent inverse of capital N plus one minus tangent inverse of one.

Now let capital N go to infinity. Tangent inverse of capital N plus one approaches pi over two. And tangent inverse of one is pi over four. So the sum is pi over two minus pi over four, which is pi over four.
The entire difficulty of this problem is a single act of recognition. Spotting the a minus b over one plus a b pattern hiding inside the innocent looking one plus n plus n squared.
Let us close Part three with the four ways students bleed marks in this block, and the one opening move that prevents most of them.
Loss one, the headline error. Forgetting the plus or minus pi when x y exceeds one. The fix is a habit, compute x y first, on every single arctangent sum.
And if x y does exceed one, decide the sign of the correction from the signs of x and y before you even touch the formula. Both positive means add pi, both negative means subtract pi.
Loss two, ignoring the multiple angle domain conditions. Two tangent inverse of x equals tangent inverse of two x over one minus x squared only when the absolute value of x is less than one.

And three sine inverse of x equals sine inverse of three x minus four x cubed only when the absolute value of x is at most one half. Quoting a multiple angle identity outside its fence is the number one proof failure.
Loss three, the sign slip in the difference formula. The denominator there is one plus x y, with a plus, the exact opposite of the minus in the sum. Anchor which is which.

Loss four, mis reading a telescoping series. The whole game is rewriting each term as tangent inverse of a minus tangent inverse of b so consecutive terms cancel. If your split does not cancel, your choice of a and b is wrong.

<whisper>And the single opening move that ties it together. Compute x y first, always. That one number instantly tells you whether you are in the clean case or the plus or minus pi case, and the pi omission is by far the most expensive mistake in this chapter.
This final subtopic turns the identities into tools, and it opens with the picture, the graphs of the inverse functions.

Here is the one idea that generates every graph. Take the parent function, say y equals sine x on its branch minus pi over two to pi over two, and flip it across the line y equals x. What you get is y equals sine inverse x.
See the reflection. The faint curve is the parent sine on its branch. The bold curve is its mirror image across the dashed diagonal, and that mirror is sine inverse.

The reflection does one crucial thing. It swaps domain and range. So the inverse's domain is the parent's range, and the inverse's range is the parent's domain. That fact you memorised in Part one is now something you can literally see.
Shape is preserved under the mirror. A monotonic increasing curve stays increasing. Sine inverse and tangent inverse keep their origin symmetry, so they are odd.
Cosine inverse and cotangent inverse fall from left to right. Tangent inverse flattens toward horizontal asymptotes at plus and minus pi over two, and cotangent inverse toward zero and pi.
Group them by trend. Increasing are sine inverse, tangent inverse and secant inverse. Decreasing are cosine inverse, cotangent inverse and cosecant inverse.
So the graph is not new information. It is the domain and range swap from Part one, made visible in a single reflection.

To evaluate $\cos(\sin^{-1}x)$, name the inner angle: let $\theta=\sin^{-1}x$, so $\sin\theta=x$.

board_events.text: JEE Main: substitution to a double-angle
Simplify $\sin^{-1}\dfrac{2x}{1+x^2}$ for $|x|\le 1$. Substitute $x=\tan\theta$, so $\theta=\tan^{-1}x$, $|\theta|\le\tfrac{\pi}{4}$.
This is the bridge to Part 3's multiple-angle identity: same result, reached by substitution.
The fence $|x|\le 1$ is what keeps $2\theta$ inside the sine branch.
Outside the fence the answer becomes $\pi - 2\tan^{-1}x$ (positive $x$): the branch fold returns.
JEE Advanced: perfect-square half-angles
Simplify $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{\cos x}{1+\sin x}$ for $x\in\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$. Convert to half-angles.
The whole problem is spotting that $1+\sin x$ is a perfect square of half-angles.
Divide top and bottom by $\cos\tfrac{x}{2}$ to expose the $\tan\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{4}-\tfrac{x}{2}\right)$ form.
Four losses + two habits
One: reading the wrong ratio. $\cos(\sin^{-1}x)=\sqrt{1-x^2}$ but $\tan(\sin^{-1}x)=\tfrac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$.
Set up the triangle once and label all three sides before reading anything.
Two: dropping the sign/branch. The triangle gives magnitudes; restore the sign from the range.
Three: wrong substitution. $\sqrt{1+x^2}\Rightarrow x=\tan\theta$, not $\sin\theta$.
Four: forgetting the validity window. $\sin^{-1}\tfrac{2x}{1+x^2}=2\tan^{-1}x$ only for $|x|\le 1$.
Habit one: for any $f(g^{-1}(x))$, draw the triangle immediately, don't hunt for a formula.
Habit two: name the radical's signature and substitute on reflex.
Your complete Chapter 02 toolkit
This restates the whole chapter's machinery in one place; it is your complete revision toolkit.

segments.text: A J E E Main level simplification that shows the substitution method and the multiple angle identity are the same thing from two directions.

Simplify sine inverse of two x over one plus x squared, for the absolute value of x at most one. Substitute x equals tangent theta, so theta is tangent inverse x, and the fence puts the absolute value of theta at most pi over four.
Now the argument transforms. Two x over one plus x squared becomes two tangent theta over one plus tangent squared theta, which is exactly the double angle formula for sine, giving sine of two theta.
So we have sine inverse of sine of two theta. And this equals two theta directly, because two theta stays inside the sine branch, minus pi over two to pi over two, thanks to the fence.
Convert back. Two theta is two tangent inverse x. So sine inverse of two x over one plus x squared equals two tangent inverse x.
Notice what happened. This is exactly the multiple angle identity from Part three, but reached here by substitution instead of by doubling. Two roads, one destination.
And the fence earns its keep. The condition, absolute value of x at most one, is precisely what keeps two theta inside the sine branch so the cancellation is legal.
Step outside the fence and the answer changes. For x beyond one and positive, it becomes pi minus two tangent inverse x. The branch fold from every earlier subtopic returns right on cue.
The closing worked example is a J E E Advanced simplification whose entire difficulty is one clever recognition.
Simplify tangent inverse of cosine x over one plus sine x, for x in minus pi over two to pi over two. The move is to convert everything into half angles.
Two half angle facts. Cosine x equals cosine squared x over two minus sine squared x over two. And crucially, one plus sine x is a perfect square, cosine x over two plus sine x over two, all squared.

Now the fraction. The numerator factors as a difference of squares, cosine x over two minus sine x over two times cosine plus sine. One factor cancels the squared denominator, leaving cosine x over two minus sine x over two, over cosine x over two plus sine x over two.
Divide top and bottom by cosine x over two. That gives one minus tangent x over two, over one plus tangent x over two, which is exactly the tangent of pi over four minus x over two.
So the outer tangent inverse cancels the tangent, and the answer is pi over four minus x over two. A clean linear expression.
The whole problem hinges on one recognition, that one plus sine x is a perfect square of half angles. Miss that and you are stuck. See it and the rest is mechanical.
And the enabling step to remember, divide top and bottom by cosine x over two, which is what exposes the tangent of pi over four minus x over two form.
Let us close this subtopic with the four ways students slip on graphs and composites, and the two habits that fix them.

Loss one, reading the wrong ratio off the triangle. Cosine of sine inverse x is root one minus x squared, but tangent of sine inverse x is x over root one minus x squared. Same triangle, different ratios.
The fix is discipline. Set up the triangle once and label all three sides before you read anything at all.
Loss two, dropping the sign or the branch. The triangle only gives you magnitudes. For negative x, or for angles in the second quadrant, you must restore the correct sign from the range.
Loss three, the wrong substitution. A root one plus x squared calls for x equals tangent theta, not sine theta. The wrong choice leaves an expression that will not simplify.

Loss four, forgetting the validity window after simplifying. Sine inverse of two x over one plus x squared equals two tangent inverse x only for the absolute value of x at most one. Outside, it becomes pi minus two tangent inverse x.
Now the two habits that make this subtopic mechanical. Habit one, for any composite of a function and an inverse, draw the triangle immediately. Do not hunt through memory for a formula.

<whisper>Habit two, for any expression with a radical, name its signature and substitute on reflex. Root one minus for sine, root one plus for tangent, root minus one for secant. These two habits turn most of this subtopic into routine.
Now the complete toolkit for Chapter two, gathered in one place. This is a restatement, not a re teaching, so let it wash over you as a checklist.

Recall the six branches. Sine inverse and cosine inverse take inputs from minus one to one. Tangent inverse and cotangent inverse take all reals. Secant inverse and cosecant inverse need absolute value at least one, and each drops one point.

Recall the fold backs. Sine of pi minus theta equals sine theta. Cosine of two pi minus theta equals cosine theta. Tangent of theta plus or minus pi equals tangent theta. These fold any angle into its branch.
Recall the negative argument split. Sine, tangent and cosecant flip the sign. Cosine, secant and cotangent use pi minus. Branch shape decides which.
Recall the complementary law. Each co pair, sine with cosine, tangent with cotangent, cosecant with secant, sums to pi over two.
Recall the arctangent sum and difference. Sum uses one minus x y in the denominator, add plus or minus pi when x y exceeds one. Difference uses one plus x y.
Recall the multiple angle family. Two tangent inverse x has three faces, and the triple angle forms carry tight fences on x.
And recall the composite and conversion results, the tangent triangle values plus the two signature simplifications.
That is the whole chapter, restated in one place as a single revision toolkit. Keep this board as your night before checklist.

board_events.text: Self-combination, fenced by a domain
Put $\theta = \tan^{-1}x$, so $\tan\theta = x$, $\theta\in\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$. Use the double-angle sine.
So $2\tan^{-1}x = \sin^{-1}\dfrac{2x}{1+x^2}$ exactly when $|x|\le 1$. Outside that, a $\pi-$ fold is needed.
The triple uses $\sin 3\theta = 3\sin\theta - 4\sin^3\theta$ with $\theta=\sin^{-1}x$.
Every multiple-angle identity carries a domain fence, and that fence IS the exam question.
Convert any inverse; match any radical
Conversions stated for $x\in(0,1]$; adjust by sign/branch otherwise.
Each substitution turns a radical into a squared identity: $1-\sin^2=\cos^2$, $1+\tan^2=\sec^2$, $\sec^2-1=\tan^2$.
Match the radical to its substitution; the wrong choice leaves an un-simplifiable mess.
The whole chapter on one card
Branches: 'sin & tan hug zero; cos & cot climb to pi.' Sec drops half-pi, cosec drops zero.
$f^{-1}(f(\theta))=\theta$ only if $\theta$ is in the branch, else fold. 'Check the cage, fold the angle.'
Self-map: 'sin, tan, cosec flip the sign; cos, sec, cot reflect through $\pi$.' 'Co-pair adds to ninety.'
Combination: 'compute $xy$ first'; $xy\gt1\Rightarrow$ add a $\pi$. Sum over one-minus, difference over one-plus.
Composites: 'draw the triangle, read the ratio.' Root one-minus $\Rightarrow$ sine; root one-plus $\Rightarrow$ tan; root minus-one $\Rightarrow$ sec.
